papers.title: First Experimental Results of Space Object Detection Using the InteRFeX Array
papers.abstract: This paper presents the first experimental validation of InteRFeX, a non-uniform receive only (passive) array located at the Nova Systems Space Precinct in Peterborough, Australia, designed for space domain awareness applications. It operates over a frequency range of 70 to 300 MHz and is capable of functioning in a range of observational modes, including as a coherent passive bistatic radar for space surveillance, which is the focus of this work. InteRFeX exploits commercial broadcast transmissions as illuminators of opportunity, combining cross-ambiguity function processing for bistatic range and range-rate retrieval with MUSIC-based direction-of-arrival (DoA) estimation for angular localization. The International Space Station (ISS) serves as the experimental target, with measurements evaluated against Two-Line Element (TLE) orbit predictions. Taking advantage of the dual-polarized array, all four reference--surveillance polarization combinations are evaluated, revealing differences in detection rate and mean signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) over the observation pass, with bistatic-range RMSEs of approximately 1 km relative to the TLE-derived reference. Independently, the MUSIC-based DoA estimates exhibit a mean angular separation of approximately $0.45^\circ$ from the TLE-derived reference directions. The angular deviations are further decomposed into along-track and cross-track components, enabling a more detailed characterization of the DoA offsets relative to the TLE-derived reference trajectory. The processing framework also includes a first-order bistatic link-budget analysis to estimate the expected SNR over the observation geometry. These results demonstrate the feasibility of passive-radar space domain awareness using radio-interferometric array technology and establish the proposed signal-processing pipeline as a basis for a dedicated coherent passive-radar mode within InteRFeX.

papers.title: Magnetic connectivity from the Sun to the Earth with MHD models II. Impact of input magnetic maps
papers.abstract: Connectivity estimation needs to be fast and thus usually relies on semi-empirical models. We previously established that optimised magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) models can also be used to derive magnetic connectivity, yielding good results, especially for complex configurations. However, the modelling is not the only factor that can impact the connectivity estimation. Models' results, both semi-empirical and MHD, depend heavily on the input data used to drive the simulation. In order to quantify this impact on our connectivity estimation, we used 20 different maps by four providers. We selected the period of July 2019, which corresponds to Carrington rotation (CR) number 2219, because it had already been studied in a previous paper. It corresponds to a period of minimum activity, meaning minimal interference from transient structures, but with a high-speed stream and several polarity switches. We have compared our results with in situ data from ACE and developed several visualisation techniques to validate connectivity not only for a specific date but also for a full CR. The choice of the input magnetic map drastically affects the connectivity estimates, with global scores going from 28% global agreement to 63% in the most extreme case. The HMI and GONG maps consistently gave the best connectivity estimations, with more than 50% correct results of the full CR. For this specific period, the GONG-ADAPT maps yielded the least reliable results, with a score below 35%. This is not surprising, as we have shown before that COCONUT required parameter adjustments for these maps. However, WSO maps which showed poor coronal agreement actually provided good connectivity estimates, showing that the Heliospheric Current Sheet (HCS) location is in the end the most crucial parameter for connectivity. Consistent data over a full Carrington rotation are to be favored compared to daily.
